title: Working at Height
blurb: Why falls from low heights matter, and how to avoid working at height or do it safely with the right equipment.
siteNotes: What access equipment the venue has (step-ladders, platform steps, towers) and where it is kept
Who is allowed to use the higher equipment, and who inspects it
Who to report unsafe access or damaged equipment to
legalNotes: From BHB-10MT-29. Work at Height Regulations 2005: avoid working at height where possible, use the right equipment, and take care in selecting and using it. HSE guidance on ladders and step-ladders (three points of contact, do not overreach).

CHECK: the trainer says falls from height are the single biggest cause of workplace deaths in the UK, and cause thousands of serious injuries. HSE statistics have long listed falls from height as the biggest cause of fatal workplace injuries; confirm the latest HSE annual figures before this wording is relied on.
CHECK: the trainer is for maintenance and housekeeping staff. Confirm the venue has rules on who may use towers and platforms, and on who inspects ladders and steps.

cards.title: Working at Height
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- say what working at height means
- avoid it, or use the right equipment
- stop and report when access looks unsafe

cards.title: Falls hurt, from any height
cards.body: Falls from height are the single biggest cause of workplace deaths, and they cause thousands of serious injuries every year. Many of those falls are from quite low heights: a step-ladder, a chair, the edge of a stage. You do not have to be up a scaffold to be at risk.

items.label: many falls are from quite low heights

cards.title: Any fall likely to injure
cards.body: "Working at height" means any task where you could fall a distance likely to cause injury. The first thing to ask is whether you can avoid it altogether. Can the job be done from the ground, with a longer-handled tool for instance?

items.title: Ask first
items.text: Can it be done from the ground?

cards.title: The right kit, used properly
cards.body: Standing on a chair, a box, a bar stool or a pile of furniture to reach something is one of the most common ways people fall. Never do it. Use a proper step-ladder for short jobs, or a platform or tower for longer ones.

left.title: Use
items: A proper step-ladder for short jobs
A platform or tower for longer jobs

cards.title: Three points, no overreach
cards.body: Keep three points of contact. Do not overreach or overload yourself. Be aware of what is around and below you: other people, doors that might open and hazards underfoot.

items.title: No overreaching
items.text: Move the ladder, do not stretch

items.title: Look around
items.text: People, doors and hazards below you

cards.title: Stop and report
cards.body: If the access looks unsafe, or you are not sure you can do it safely, stop and report it rather than taking a chance. A few minutes setting up properly is nothing compared to weeks off with a broken bone.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Ask first: can the job be done from the ground?
- Never stand on a chair, box, bar stool or furniture.
- Use a proper step-ladder, or a platform or tower for longer jobs.
- Three points of contact. Do not overreach. Watch people, doors and hazards.
- Unsafe or unsure: stop and report it.

cards.q: Falls from height are the biggest cause of what in workplaces?
options: Minor cuts
Late finishes
Deaths
Back strain
cards.why: Falls from height are the single biggest cause of workplace deaths.

cards.q: Many falls happen from quite low heights, not just high ones.
cards.why: A step-ladder, a chair or the edge of a stage is enough. You do not have to be up a scaffold.

cards.q: What is the FIRST thing to ask before working at height?
options: Which ladder is nearest to hand
Whether a colleague can hold the steps
Whether it can be avoided by working from the ground
How quickly the job can be done
cards.why: First ask whether you can avoid working at height altogether, such as using a longer-handled tool from the ground.

cards.q: Standing on a chair or box to reach something is acceptable if you're quick.
cards.why: Standing on a chair, box, bar stool or furniture is one of the most common ways people fall. Never do it.

cards.q: For a longer task at height you should use…
options: A bar stool and a steady hand
A stack of two sturdy chairs
A sturdy box on a table
A proper platform or tower
cards.why: Use a proper step-ladder for short jobs or a platform or tower for longer ones.

cards.q: You should be aware of people and doors around and below you.
cards.why: Be aware of other people, doors that might open and hazards underfoot.

cards.q: If access looks unsafe, what should you do?
options: Carry on carefully and report it later
Ask someone to take over without saying why
Use something sturdier to stand on
Stop and report it
cards.why: Stop and report it rather than taking a chance.

cards.q: "Working at height" means any task where you could…
options: Get tired from a long task
Get cold in a high place
Fall a distance likely to cause injury
Be in a hurry to finish
cards.why: It means any task where you could fall a distance likely to cause injury.

cards.q: Overreaching while up a ladder is a common cause of falls.
cards.why: Do not overreach or overload yourself while up there.

cards.q: Improvising with whatever's to hand is fine as long as it feels stable.
cards.why: Never improvise. Use the right, well-maintained equipment for the task.
